newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Germany is last Europe major to revalue gold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany is last Europe major to revalue gold.

text.p: Germany will become the last major European Union (EU) power to value its gold in a way that brings it closer to market prices, if a finance ministery plan announced on Thursday is adopted.
Most European Union(EU) countries have already changed the way they value their reserves so that they at least reflect the market.
But Germany had stuck to a more traditional and ultra-prudent approach of valuing based on purchase price.

France switched from a fixed price gold reserve valuation in 1975 followed by Italy a year later. Austria and the Netherlands both began pricing on a marker basis in 1978. Britain acted in 1979 and Portugal and Spain in 1981.
Belgium was the last original EU member to change, in 1991.
"The difference is that Germany has linked revaluing gold reserves to a budget problem," said bullion market analyst Andy Smith at Union Bank of Switzerland.
On Thursday Finance Minister Theo Waigel announced plans for the Bundesbank to revalue its reserves of nearly 3,000 tonnes from $95 an ounce closer to the market price, now just $350.
It could be a boost - on paper - to Germany's exchequer of up to 40 billion marks.
Waigel's move appeared meant to plug a hole in the budget and keep Germany on course for European Monetary Union at the beginning of 1999.
The gold market was stunned by the announcement that one of the staunchest conservatives on bullion reserves was contemplating changing gold into just another asset.
"This is a structural break for the market," Smith said. "Now (as far as Germany is concerned) gold has lost its innocence. It has become an other asset which has to perform."
The price fell by only a stoical few dollars in the week's range around $346-$348 per ounce.
"A few years ago this would have knocked $20-$30 off the price," a gold dealer said.
The EU central banks between them hold more than 14,000 tonnes of gold in their reserves.

The central banks of Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and Britain all told Reuters they had no plans to boost the book value of their bullion. Austria, France, Italy and Belgium had no comment.
"There is nothing to stop the other countries revaluing (reserves) to whatever they want. It just puts national credibility at stake," Smith said.
The European central banks value gold in various ways related to market prices.
The Bank of France revalues each six months to reflect market prices while the Belgians and Danes do so annually.
The Dutch Central Bank adjusts the value of its reserves every three years, basing the new total on the lowest average market price for the period minus 30 percent.
A Bank of Portugal spokesman said, "It makes no sense to revalue our reserves as the accounting value is close to the market value."
According to International Monetary Fund figures, at the end of 1996 most of the EU countries' gold reserves were on the books at well under current market value.
But some - Ireland ($397), Belgium ($385), Italy ($381), France ($371) and Denmark ($355) - were above, pending the next review, because prices had fallen last year.
The final 1996 gold market fixing price was $369.55.
Reserves are often priced in line with a formula already approved by the European Monetary Institute (EMI).
Italian "gold reserves will remain in their present conditions. There are already precise criteria for revaluations agreed at a European level with the EMI," a Bank of Italy source said.
An EU official defended Waigel's proposal saying it was in line with practice of most European central banks and by no means a way of "cooking the books," as some Gernman press comment suggested.

"What the Bundesbank would do is precisely what other central banks are doing. It is not cooking its books, quite the opposite in fact," the official said. "The continental approach is to be very cautious in gold valuation."
